{{Short description|Technique in topological data analysis}}

In [[topological data analysis]], a '''subdivision bifiltration''' is a collection of [[Filtration (mathematics)|filtered]] [[simplicial complex]]es, typically built upon a set of data points in a [[metric space]], that captures shape and density information about the underlying data set. The subdivision bifiltration relies on a natural filtration of the [[barycentric subdivision]] of a [[simplicial complex]] by [[Flag (geometry)|flags]] of minimum dimension, which encodes density information about the metric space upon which the complex is built. The subdivision bifiltration was first introduced by Donald Sheehy in 2011 as part of his doctoral thesis<ref>Sheehy, D. R. (2011). ''[http://ra.adm.cs.cmu.edu/anon/anon/2011/CMU-CS-11-121.pdf Mesh generation and geometric persistent homology]'' (Doctoral dissertation, Carnegie Mellon University).</ref> (later subsumed by a conference paper in 2012<ref>Sheehy, Donald R. 2012. “[https://donsheehy.net/research/sheehy12multicover.pdf A Multicover Nerve for Geometric Inference].” in ''CCCG: Canadian conference in computational geometry''.</ref>) as a [[Discrete modelling|discrete model]] of the [[multicover bifiltration]], a continuous construction whose underlying framework dates back to the 1970s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fejes Tóth |first=G. |date=March 1976 |title=Multiple packing and covering of the plane with circles |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01896768 |journal=Acta Mathematica Academiae == Definition ==
Let <math>T</math> be a [[simplicial complex]]. Then a nested sequence of [[simplices]] <math>\sigma_1 \subset \sigma_2 \subset \cdots \subset \sigma_k</math> of <math>T</math> is called a ''flag'' or ''chain'' of <math>T</math>. The set of all flags of <math>T</math> comprises an [[abstract simplicial complex]], known as the ''[[barycentric subdivision]]'' of <math>T</math>, denoted by <math>\operatorname{Bary}(T)</math>. The barycentric subdivision is naturally identified with a geometric subdivision of <math>T</math>, created by ''starring'' the [[Simplicial set|geometric realization]] of <math>T</math> at the [[Barycentric coordinate system|barycenter]] of each simplex.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rourke |first=C. P. |title=Introduction to piecewise-linear topology |date=1982 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |others=B. J. Sanderson |isbn=0-387-11102-6 |location=Berlin |oclc=7948164}}</ref>

There is a natural [[Filtration (mathematics)|filtration]] on <math>\operatorname{Bary}(T)</math> by considering for each [[natural number]] <math>k</math> the maximal subcomplex of <math>\operatorname{Bary}(T)</math> spanned by [[Point (geometry)|vertices]] of <math>\operatorname{Bary}(T)</math> corresponding to simplices of <math>T</math> of dimension at least <math>k-1</math>, which is denoted <math>\tilde \mathcal S (T)_k</math>. In particular, by this convention, then <math>\tilde \mathcal S (T)_1 = \operatorname{Bary}(T)</math>. Considering the sequence of nested subcomplexes given by varying the parameter <math>k</math>, we obtain a filtration on <math>\operatorname{Bary}(T)</math> known as the ''subdivision filtration.'' Since the complexes in the subdivision filtration shrink as <math>k</math> increases, we can regard it as a [[functor]] <math>\tilde \mathcal S (-): \mathbb N^\operatorname{op} \to \mathbf{Simp}</math> from the [[Opposite category|opposite]] [[posetal category]] <math>\mathbb N^\operatorname{op}</math> to the category <math>\mathbf{Simp}</math> of simplicial complexes and [[simplicial map]]s.

Let <math>P</math> be a [[partially ordered set]]. Given a simplicial filtration <math>F: P \to \mathbf{Simp}</math>, regarded as a functor from the posetal category of <math>P</math> to the category <math>\mathbf{Simp}</math>, by applying the subdivision filtration object-wise on <math>F</math>, we obtain a two-parameter filtration <math>\mathcal S (F): \mathbb N^\operatorname{op}\times P \to \mathbf{Simp}</math>, called the ''subdivision bifiltration.''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lesnick |first=Michael |date=11 March 2023 |title=Lecture notes for AMAT 840: Multiparameter Persistence |url=https://www.albany.edu/~ML644186/840_2022/Math840_Notes_22.pdf |access-date=27 March 2023}}</ref>

In particular, when we take <math>F</math> to be the [[Rips complex|Rips]] or [[Čech]] filtration, we obtain bifiltrations <math>\mathcal S \operatorname{Rips}(-)</math> and <math>\mathcal S \operatorname{\check{C}ech}(-)</math>, respectively.

== Properties ==
The subdivision-Čech bifiltration is weakly equivalent to the multicover bifiltration, implying that they have isomorphic persistent homology. A combinatorial proof of this statement was given in Sheehy's original conference paper, but a more algebraic version was presented in 2017 by Cavanna et al.<ref>{{cite book | doi=10.1137/1.9781611974782.177 | chapter=When and Why the Topological Coverage Criterion Works | title=Proceedings of the Twenty-Eighth Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms | year=2017 | last1=Cavanna | first1=Nicholas J. | last2=Gardner | first2=Kirk P. | last3=Sheehy | first3=Donald R. | pages=2679–2690 | isbn=978-1-61197-478-2 }}</ref> The ideas from Cavanna's proof were later generalized by Blumberg and Lesnick in a 2022 paper on 2-parameter persistent homology.<ref name=":0" />

By the ''size'' of a bifiltration, we mean the number of simplices in the largest complex. The subdivision-Čech bifiltration has exponential size as a function of the number of vertices.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Corbet |first1=René |last2=Kerber |first2=Michael |last3=Lesnick |first3=Michael |last4=Osang |first4=Georg |date=2023-02-20 |title=Computing the Multicover Bifiltration |journal=Discrete & Computational Geometry |volume=70 |issue=2 |pages=376–405 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s00454-022-00476-8 |pmid=37581017 |pmc=10423148 |issn=0179-5376|arxiv=2103.07823 }}</ref> This implies that its [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]] cannot be directly computed in [[Polynomial-time|polynomial time]]. However, for points in Euclidean space, the homology of subdivision-Čech can be computed in polynomial time, up to [[Weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak equivalence]], via a construction known as the ''[[rhomboid]] bifiltration.'' As a precursor to the rhomboid bifiltration, [[Herbert Edelsbrunner|Edelsbrunner]] and Osang presented in 2021 a [[Polyhedral surface|polyhedral]] [[CW complex|cell complex]] called the ''rhomboid tiling'', which they used to compute horizontal or vertices slices of the multicover bifiltration up to weak equivalence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Edelsbrunner |first1=Herbert |last2=Osang |first2=Georg |date=2021 |title=The Multi-Cover Persistence of Euclidean Balls |journal=Discrete & Computational Geometry |language=en |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=1296–1313 |doi=10.1007/s00454-021-00281-9 |issn=0179-5376 |pmc= 8550220|pmid=34720303}}</ref> This was extended a year later by Corbet et al. to the rhomboid bifiltration, which is weakly equivalent to the multicover bifiltration, but has polynomial size.<ref name=":1" />
